item.title: Uncertainty Quantification and Global Sensitivity Analysis of Patient-Specific Coronary Hemodynamics Under Unsteady Flow Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2611.31594v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Patient-specific computational models of the coronary arteries demonstrate transformative potential for physiological assessment, identifying hemodynamic markers associated with disease progression, and optimizing treatment. Unfortunately, these models rarely account for input parameter uncertainty, limiting confidence in predictions and their clinical interpretation. Herein, we present a novel uncertainty quantification-finite element framework that integrates computationally efficient techniques to characterize and propagate uncertainty through patient-specific coronary simulations under unsteady flow conditions. Principal component analysis characterized variability in pulsatile coronary velocity waveforms, while uncertainty in blood pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate is represented through probability distributions. Polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) enabled efficient uncertainty propagation and global sensitivity analysis across three patient-specific models, quantifying variability in time-averaged wall shear stress (WSS), oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index. Fourth-order PCE emulators converged across all three patients, yielding analyses of 505 models per patient, with median coefficients of variation ranging from 0.15-0.20 for time-averaged WSS, 0.54-0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28-0.38 for cross-flow index, highlighting greater relative uncertainty in multidirectional WSS metrics. Global sensitivity analysis revealed that time-averaged WSS variability was governed by the individual effects of velocity and blood viscosity, with parameter interactions contributing <2% of total variance. In contrast, velocity waveform uncertainty dominated variability in the oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index, with higher-order parameter interactions accounting for 20.7-34.5% and 26.6-37.8% of total variance, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Usman, Nafis M. Arefin, Akil Narayan, Lucas H. Timmins

item.title: The Contrast Order: An Order-Based Image Quality Criterion for Nonlinear Beamformers
item.description: arXiv:2602.01622v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many modern ultrasound beamformers report improved image quality when evaluated using classical criteria like the contrast ratio and contrast-to-noise ratio, which are based on summary statistics of regions of interest (ROIs). However, nonlinear beamformers and post-processing methods can substantially alter these statistics, raising concerns that the reported improvements may reflect changes in dynamic range or remapping rather than a reflection of true information gain, such as clutter suppression. Introduced recently, the generalized contrast-to-noise ratio (gCNR) is designed to address these concerns, but it requires implementation-dependent density estimation. We propose herein a new, simpler, image quality criterion, called the contrast order (CO), defined as the expected value of the sign of the difference in brightness between two ROIs. The CO is invariant under all strictly monotonic transformations of the image values, as it depends only on their relative ordering, and is interpretable as the probability that one ROI is brighter than the other minus the probability that it is darker. Unlike the gCNR, the CO has a simple unbiased estimator whose variance provably decreases with the number of samples in each ROI. We further propose the effective contrast ratio (ECR), which calibrates the contrast order to the familiar contrast ratio such that the two coincide under ideal Rayleigh-speckle statistics. Together, the CO and ECR provide order- and sign-preserving, dynamic-range-invariant criteria for evaluating lesion contrast, offering a principled alternative to classical and newer image quality criteria when assessing modern beamformers.
item.dc:creator: Dongwoon Hyun, Samuel Beuret, Jeremy J. Dahl

item.title: A unified perspective on wavelength selection for molecular composition inference from diffuse spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2606.23223v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optical monitoring of living tissue targeting quantification of molecular composition is an active area of research. In the case of broadband spectroscopy, one can attempt to extract molecular, or more precisely, chromophore concentration from a broad-range spectrum of the reflected light. However, selecting the shortest wavelength range sufficient for quantitative optical monitoring remains an open problem. Various wavelength optimization methods are scattered throughout the literature, however, there is no unified view to date. Our work's motivation is to construct a wavelength selection framework by unifying existing selection approaches and propose a novel projection-based method that allows for the pre-identification of a wavelength range that is adequate for the final selection. The framework specifically focuses on proposing different methods that quantify match or mismatch between the chosen light-matter interaction model, defined by the chosen endmembers (e.g. molecular chromophores), and the measured intensity from the spectroscopic data. To evaluate the framework, we perform a retrospective analysis on a broadband spectroscopy dataset of piglets during an induced hypoxia-ischemia state. Overall, we show that our novel projection-based method can be used for band selection, and that existing approaches can be used in conjunction to select an optimal minimal wavelength set that satisfies biophysical model constraints.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Scibilia, Marcel Rosier, Luca Giannoni, Pietro Ricci, Fr\'ed\'eric Lange, Francesco S. Pavone, Ilias Tachtsidis, Daniel Rueckert, Ivan Ezhov

item.title: Certificate-Based Verification of Pulsed Field Ablation Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.18148v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Computational models of cardiac pulsed field ablation predict the lesion as the tissue where the electric field exceeds a lethal threshold. Their numerical error is rarely bounded, and automated pipelines increasingly run them without an expert checking each result. To verify each run, we separate the question "was the stated model solved correctly?" from the solver that answers it. An untrusted solver returns its answer with a certificate, which consists of a potential with the correct electrode and ground values and an exactly charge-conserving current. A small independent checker verifies the certificate against a written specification of the physics. Using the Prager-Synge hypercircle theorem evaluated in ball arithmetic, it turns the certificate into guaranteed two-sided bounds on the impedance and on the root-mean-square field of every tile of a lesion map, also over a range of blood/tissue conductivity ratios. The bounds cover numerical error only; whether the model describes tissue is a question of validation. A vectorized version of the checker takes about a tenth of our solver's time. For a focal electrode in contact, the tile-resolved depth at 1000 V and 700 V/cm is proven to lie in 3.50-3.75 mm for every ratio from 1.7 to 3.75. For a bipolar catheter, certified depths overlap published in-vivo depths. Where they differ from a published reference model, the certificates prove that the difference is not our numerical error. We compare the certificate with a grid convergence study on the same solver. On graded grids, the study is sharper for local fields but remains an estimate. On uniform grids, it fails to converge at the electrode edge, where the certificate still gives a valid bracket. Solvers that deliberately solve equations other than the specified ones pass the grid convergence study, but the certificates refute the impedances they report or leave them unsupported.
